items: We got Samsung’s private AI cloud, referred to as “SPAC” in the code, working with AI select on a Galaxy S26 Ultra running One UI 9.5 Beta 1, producing more accurate calendar event extraction than its standard processing.
Code references show SPAC supports Google’s Gemma 4 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 (used in our test) and appears to route encrypted requests through a third-party relay to hide user identity.

In our test, SPAC only pulled one event out of the five listed, but Samsung’s code indicates multi-event support. It also suggests photo editing, live translation, and writing tools could adopt SPAC next.

blocks.text: Yesterday, we reported that Samsung is building a private cloud for Galaxy AI. The system, called “SPAC” in Samsung’s code, appears to closely follow Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. At the time, SPAC wasn’t switched on for our Galaxy S26 Ultra. Now we’ve managed to get it running, and the result is better than what Galaxy AI does today.
APK teardown
This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →
AI select used SPAC to add an event to our calendar

AI select, part of the Samsung Capture app, can pull details from your screen and suggest actions, like adding an event to your calendar. We pointed it at a Google search result listing upcoming Lollapalooza dates and tapped “Add event.”
On One UI 9.5 Beta 1 on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, this normally opens Samsung Calendar with fields filled in from the selected text.

The result was a bit of a mess: the event was titled “Course Reservation” for some reason. It selected the Mumbai entry for the dates but added multiple locations to the location field. Clearly, the “Lollapalooza India” context was lost.
Once we managed to turn on SPAC for AI select, the same selection and tap took a different route.

AI select sent the selection to Samsung’s SPAC servers, and after a few noticeable seconds of processing (which were missing before), Samsung Capture showed its own “Add event” sheet with a cleaner entry: “Lollapalooza India,” January 23, 2027, at Mahalaxmi Race Course, Mumbai. AI select managed to get the correct title, date, and venue for the calendar entry, without any edits from our end.

Admittedly, the result wasn’t perfect. The page listed five Lollapalooza editions, and SPAC returned only the first, possibly either because of our device location (Mumbai) or simply because it was the first entry in the list. Samsung’s code supports adding several events at once, so this could change by the time the feature goes live for users.
SPAC’s privacy design appears to be in place

SPAC’s code describes several privacy layers, including a third-party relay that hides where a request comes from and a public-style record of Samsung’s server software. When AI select used SPAC, our phone did not look up Samsung’s AI server directly. That’s pretty much how this design is supposed to work: the phone sends the request to a relay, and the relay forwards the encrypted request to SPAC, so the AI server only sees the request, not who sent it.

The code lists Google’s Gemma 4 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.6 as AI select’s two SPAC options, and our test used Qwen 3.6. Your phone will only send the model’s name with the request, so we can’t confirm which model actually answered.
What this means for Galaxy AI

blocks.alt: Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra Galaxy AI Now Brief

blocks.text: Stephen Radochia / Android Authority

The demo is small, but it’s the first sign that Samsung’s private AI cloud is real and not just code in the platform. A Galaxy phone can already send it a request and get a useful answer, although all of this is still very much a beta.

If Samsung goes ahead, AI select could be one of the first Galaxy AI features to run on SPAC, with photo editing, live translation, and writing tools possibly following. It’s also not clear yet whether SPAC-powered features would be free or paid as part of Galaxy AI Premium.
We’ve reached out to Samsung for comment on SPAC and will update this article if we hear back.

Got a MediaTek, Exynos, or Pixel device? Here are 11 tips for emulation

From specific settings to alternative emulators, here's what you can try on your non-Snapdragon device.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 4:00 AM ET

•

•

Nick Fernandez / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

There’s no shortage of emulators on Android, letting you play everything from Atari 2600 and NES games to PC and Nintendo Switch titles. We’ve even seen Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and Switch 2 emulators in recent times.

It’s fair to say, though, that devices with Qualcomm Snapdragon chips are generally the best for emulation. Phones and handhelds with MediaTek, Google Tensor, or Samsung Exynos silicon often suffer from worse performance and compatibility with new emulators as a result. Thankfully, there are plenty of tips you can try if you’re struggling with emulation on your MediaTek-powered device, Exynos-toting Galaxy phone, or Google Pixel.

Readers' poll

What's the best tip for emulation on Android?

0 votes

1. Use Vulkan rather than OpenGL (or ANGLE)

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

One of the most enduring tips for running emulators on non-Snapdragon devices is to switch the graphics renderer from OpenGL to Vulkan. Vulkan generally performs better than OpenGL, so you should get a speed boost by making the switch. This isn’t always the case, but it’s still one of the first things you should try if you’re having performance problems in an emulator.

It’s also worth noting that Samsung’s and Google’s chips don’t have great OpenGL support in the first place. Instead, they use a “wrapper” called ANGLE to translate OpenGL calls to Vulkan. Some emulators offer ANGLE as an option in their settings. If an emulator doesn’t, you can enable ANGLE via developer options and leave the emulator on the OpenGL renderer. However, our own tests show that ANGLE can cause major issues on Pixel phones.

2. Turn down a few settings

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Is the emulated game running on your device, just slowly? Then there are several ways to speed it up. For one, you can try lowering the game’s rendering/internal resolution. This is usually set to 1x by default, but some emulators like ARMSX3 let you scale it down to 0.75x, 0.5x, and even 0.25x. The game will definitely look rougher as a result, but it’s worth a shot if your device’s GPU is taking a beating.

Another option worth pursuing in some emulators is frame skipping. As the name implies, this skips a certain number of frames (e.g., every other frame) so the game can keep running at closer to full speed. You can also try lowering the target frame rate if the game or emulator offers this option. After all, what’s the point of choosing 60fps if your device can’t maintain that frame rate in the first place?

3. Try an alternative emulator or fork

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

One of my favorite tips if you’re having emulator problems of any kind is to simply try a different emulator. AetherSX2 not running your favorite PS2 game? Then try NetherSX2 or ARMSX2. GameHub not running a specific PC game? You can always try GameNative, Winlator, or Winlator Ludashi.

There are limits to this approach, though. Some consoles only have one or two high-quality Android emulators, as is the case with the GameCube (Dolphin) and PSP (PPSSPP). Many advanced emulators also target Snapdragon-powered devices first, only improving support for MediaTek and other non-Snapdragon platforms down the line. Still, we highly recommend trying a different emulator if you’re having performance or compatibility problems.

It’s also worth noting that there are several forks of existing emulators that are optimized for MediaTek chips and other silicon. For example, we’ve seen MaliBridge and Winlator Mali for PC gaming, as well as XenDroid-Mali for Xbox 360 emulation. I’d urge caution before installing any unknown fork you come across, though.

4. Try emulating a different platform altogether

Trying to emulate a specific game, but it’s not working on your non-Snapdragon device? Switching to another emulator for the same platform is one option, but you could also try emulating a different platform altogether.

For example, a ton of games were released on both the PS2 and the original Xbox, and many of these titles also came to the GameCube. So if the PS2 version of a game isn’t giving you a great experience, you should definitely try the Xbox or GameCube version via HakuX or Dolphin, respectively.

This also applies to Xbox 360 and PS3 emulation. These consoles are still a pain to emulate on anything other than Snapdragon silicon, but some of their games came to PC as well. That means you might have better luck running these titles via GameNative, DroidDeck, or other PC “emulators.”

5. Use the system driver instead of Turnip

Robert Triggs / Android Authority

Custom Turnip drivers are all the rage in the emulation scene, as they deliver performance improvements and bug fixes over Qualcomm’s official GPU drivers. However, it’s worth stressing that Turnip drivers are only meant for Snapdragon-powered devices. You simply can’t use them on a phone, handheld, or tablet with a non-Snapdragon processor.

That’s why the team behind popular PC gaming app GameNative previously recommended sticking with the system driver instead of switching to Turnip on a MediaTek, Exynos, or Tensor device. This also applies to other emulators that support custom GPU drivers.

6. MediaTek users can try Vortek and PanVK

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Vivo X100 Ultra - Telephoto macro

Owners of non-Snapdragon devices can’t use custom Turnip drivers, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t similar options out there. Two of the most prominent are Vortek and PanVK, both of which target Mali GPUs.

The original creator of Winlator developed and released Vortek, a compatibility layer that sits on top of your device’s default graphics driver. GameNative and Winlator have previously integrated Vortek into their apps, and some users reported significant improvements on MediaTek devices. So it’s worth a shot if your emulator of choice supports it.

Meanwhile, PanVK has emerged as an alternative Vulkan driver for Mali graphics chips. We’ve seen a few PanVK projects, targeting everything from the budget Mali-G57 GPU to the Mali-G1 Ultra in recent flagship Dimensity chips. Neither Vortek nor PanVK appears to have had the same impact as Turnip did for Snapdragon chipsets, but they’re still worth trying in some emulators.

7. Exynos users can try the RADV driver

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Exynos users already had the ExynosTools suite, which is effectively a Vulkan translation layer for Exynos-powered Galaxy devices. But the open-source RADV driver arrived on Samsung Exynos devices earlier this month, too.

RADV for Samsung Xclipse is a port of the open-source Vulkan driver for AMD GPUs. Our own testing shows that this driver isn’t a silver bullet for Switch emulation, but it brought major performance gains in games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. We’ve also seen online reports that the driver delivers fixes and performance improvements in some PC games. So add this to your list if you’ve got an Exynos-powered device.

8. Use MaliSX2 for PS2 games

ARMSX2 GitHub

NetherSX2 has long been the go-to PS2 emulator on Android, rising from the ashes of the abandoned AetherSX2. However, ARMSX2 has since arrived on Android and is arguably the best PS2 emulator on the platform. It recently debuted MaliSX2, which could be a game-changer for some users.

MaliSX2 is a Vulkan driver for devices with Mali GPUs, and it ships in ARMSX2 v2.8.3 and newer. You can find it by tapping Settings > Renderer, and the ARMSX2 team promises major boosts in some games. The team claimed that Ace Combat 4 and 5, which were previously unplayable with the stock driver, ran at full speed on a device with budget-tier Mali-G57 graphics.

This driver isn’t restricted to PS2 games, either. The team has confirmed that it’s coming to Dolphin and HakuX, although our own experience with a pre-release Dolphin build suggests MaliSX2 might not be an upgrade in some games just yet.

9. Try a native port instead of the emulated version

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

We’ve seen an explosion of games being unofficially ported to Android in 2026, largely thanks to generative AI. Everything from Skyrim and Need for Speed: Underground 2 to Donkey Kong Bananza and Tears of the Kingdom has been recompiled for mobile devices.

So it’s worth trying a native port of a game instead of emulating it. These unofficial ports still require you to supply the game ROM or ISO, though. We also have to caution that some vibe-coded “ports” are little more than an emulated game with a home screen icon, so you can’t expect better performance from these shoddy ports compared to the emulated version.

You should also be careful with these projects in general, as you’ll undoubtedly find bad actors spreading malware via dodgy ports. That said, I highly recommend checking the Gaming Emporium website for a regularly updated list of new Android ports.

10. Check Reddit for help

Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority

This sounds obvious, but you should definitely check Reddit to see if anyone has found solutions for emulating a specific console or game. It might just be a case of tweaking a couple of settings to get things running smoothly.

Subreddits worth checking include r/EmulationOnAndroid and r/EmulationMediatekMali. The latter is particularly great for getting help, but it’s also a showcase of games and emulators that run well on MediaTek hardware. So even if you’re not struggling with a specific title, it’s a good way to find games that are likely to run on your device.

11. Accept that you can’t run bleeding-edge emulators

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Even if you try every tip on this list, bleeding-edge emulators simply don’t play nicely with non-Snapdragon silicon. Just look at the first Switch 2 emulators, which generally don’t support MediaTek, Exynos, or Tensor chips.

It usually takes months (if not longer) for these projects to adequately support non-Snapdragon processors. So you’ll often have to accept that you can’t run that shiny new emulator straight away, no matter what you do.

Mobile

Morphe v2.4.0 beats Google to bringing YouTube videos to your Android Auto screen

It only shows up when your vehicle is parked.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 3:50 AM ET

•

•

Hadlee Simons / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Morphe v2.4.0 is out, and it adds support for playing YouTube videos on Android Auto and other in-car entertainment platforms.

• YouTube shows up in the Android Auto launcher when the car is parked.

• Along with this, Morphe’s version of YouTube and YouTube Music also get a host of playability improvements.

Morphe is a popular open-source tool for modding popular Android apps to add features and remove ads from YouTube, YouTube Music, and other media streaming apps. In the last major update, it added 4K video downloads, surpassing download-quality limits even on the official YouTube app. Now, it’s out with another update that brings a host of changes to patched versions of Reddit, YouTube, and YouTube Music. One that truly stands out — and we hope isn’t blocked by Google — is the ability to play YouTube videos on Android Auto.

Release notes for version 2.40 of the Morphe app say a new patch now lets Morphe YouTube be seen as a “parked video app.” As a result, the app shows up in Android Auto’s app drawer, and you can watch videos directly while your vehicle isn’t moving. This is currently only available as an early access feature and also works with DriveDeck. Google itself has been working to bring a similar functionality to phones running Android 17 or newer by the end of the year. Currently, users can only listen to audio from YouTube videos on Android Auto, but the app must be controlled from the phone.

Meanwhile, another patch detects when the YouTube app is projected onto the car’s display and adjusts its layout for horizontal screens, while another one hides the navigation bar to utilize the space better. It also enables Android Auto alternatives such as DriveDeck, Gearslip, AARE, and Flywheel to browse YouTube Music’s library.

Along with this, the latest Morphe update brings several minor upgrades to both YouTube and YouTube Music that aren’t specific to Android Auto. These improvements include a new Ghost mode, similar to Incognito, where watched videos don’t show in your watch history or impact your recommendations. You can browse using Ghost mode for an entire session or launch just one video using the three-dot button — all this without having to sign out of your account.

Lyrics in YouTube Music now support a full-screen mode, along with support for custom fonts. You also get the option to disable gestures for changing tracks by swiping over the album art. Besides this, YouTube Music also gains a direct Sonos casting button that lets you stream audio directly to UPnP speakers from Sonos and other brands, so long as they’re on the same Wi-Fi.

Release notes for version 2.40 of the Morphe app say a new patch now lets Morphe YouTube be seen as a “parked video app.” As a result, the app shows up in Android Auto’s app drawer, and you can watch videos directly while your vehicle isn’t moving. Google itself has been working to bring a similar functionality to phones running Android 17 or newer by the end of the year. Currently, users can only listen to audio from YouTube videos on Android Auto, but the app must be controlled from the phone.

Meanwhile, another patch detects when the YouTube app is projected onto the car’s display and adjusts its layout for horizontal screens, while another one hides the navigation bar to utilize the space better. It also enables Android Auto alternatives such as DriveDeck, Gearslip, AARE, and Flywheel to browse YouTube Music’s library.

These improvements include a new Ghost mode, similar to Incognito, where watched videos don’t show in your watch history or impact your recommendations. You can browse using Ghost mode for an entire session or launch just one video using the three-dot button — all this without having to sign out of your account.

Lyrics in YouTube Music now support a full-screen mode, along with support for custom fonts. You also get the option to disable gestures for changing tracks by swiping over the album art. Besides this, YouTube Music also gains a direct Sonos casting button that lets you stream audio directly to UPnP speakers from Sonos and other brands, so long as they’re on the same Wi-Fi.

items.body:

Wearables and health

Oura is dropping Android 11 support in December, and users risk losing health data

Upgrading after the deadline won't bring back your health history.

Kaitlyn Cimino / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Oura will officially drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026.

• Users who don’t upgrade to Android 12 or newer by the deadline risk losing their historical health data.

• Those who remain on Android 11 may retain access to some limited historical app features.

One of the biggest benefits of wearing an Oura Ring is that the longer you use it, the more you learn about your health. From personalized annual health recaps to long-term blood pressure trends, many of Oura’s features become more useful as you build up months or even years of health data. However, some Android users could soon lose access to that history simply because of the phone they use.

Oura has updated its Android software updates support page to reveal that it will discontinue support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. Starting on that date, you’ll need a phone running Android 12 or newer to continue enjoying the full Oura app experience.

Oura will drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. If you are using an Android device, be sure to update to Android 12 or higher to ensure no loss of data or features. If you decide not to upgrade, you may still be able to use some limited historical Oura App features. Please note that if you do upgrade your smartphone system later, your historical Oura data will not carry over.

What’s particularly concerning is that this goes beyond missing out on new features and app updates. Oura warns that users who stick with Android 11 may retain access to some limited historical app features, but upgrading their phone’s operating system later will not bring their historical Oura data with them.

Essentially, putting off that software update could cost you years of sleep, activity, and recovery history.

Android 11 is now more than six years old, and Oura isn’t alone in moving away from older Android versions. Earlier this month, Google raised Android Auto’s minimum requirement to Android 11. But Oura is taking things a step further.

If your phone is still running Android 11, you should check for available software updates before December 8. Those whose phones are no longer eligible for OS updates may need to switch to a newer device. Oura also lets you export your health data through its Membership Hub, so it’s worth downloading a copy before the deadline.

items.title: Samsung phones can soon nudge you when you miss your usual charging window
items.summary: This charging reminder feature could even refer to your calendar entries for more personalized alerts.
items.body:

Mobile

Samsung phones can soon nudge you when you miss your usual charging window

This charging reminder feature could even refer to your calendar entries for more personalized alerts.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 3:11 AM ET

•

•

Ryan Haines / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Samsung’s One UI 9.5 beta can apparently tell you when you’ve missed your usual charging time.

• This alert will show up in the Settings menu and will also show how many hours of battery life you have left.

• This feature could be very useful if you’re forgetful or busy.

Samsung recently launched the One UI 9.5 beta program, allowing Galaxy S26 owners to get their hands on the latest software before the stable release. We’ve already uncovered plenty of features, but it looks like the company has a convenient charging-related feature up its sleeve.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

We’ve dug into the Device Care app (v13.9.00.12) in One UI 9.5 and discovered that Samsung phones could soon issue an alert when you’ve missed your usual charging time. We can confirm that this alert will appear when the battery is at 20-30% capacity, your phone isn’t charging, and power-saving modes are disabled. Check out the string below.

Code

<string name="suggest_appbar_charging_description">You missed your usual charging time.</string>

We’ve also uncovered strings (seen below) which show that the alert could use events in your default calendar for context. More specifically, the alert could mention that your battery might be low for a workout, movie, meeting, or show/concert at a given time. If you don’t have a matching calendar event, then the feature will fall back to the alert message seen in the string above.

Code

<string name="suggest_appbar_exercise_description">Battery may be low for your workout at %s.</string> 
<string name="suggest_appbar_meeting_description">Battery may be low for your meeting at %s.</string> 
<string name="suggest_appbar_movie_description">Battery may be low for your movie at %s.</string> 
<string name="suggest_appbar_performance_description">Battery may be low for your %1$s at %2$s.</string>

So how does this actually work? Well, you’ll first need to enable Samsung’s personalized suggestions option and have a device with One UI 9.5. The phone will then identify your preferred charging window by learning from four weeks of charging history, as retained by the Smart suggestions app. The device will then check if the current hour falls within this preferred charging window, and display the alert if this is the case. The code suggests that if you dismiss the alert, it won’t come back again for 24 hours, even if all other conditions are met. Oddly enough, we also found evidence that Samsung can remotely turn off this card.

There’s no country check, while the evidence we’ve uncovered also suggests that it won’t be exclusive to the Galaxy S27 series. So this charging alert could potentially come to older Galaxy phones in many markets.

What could these charging alerts look like?

SamMobile also posted a screenshot showing off this alert. It’s unclear whether this feature is available in some capacity or if the outlet manually enabled it by tinkering with the software. Check out the image below.

SamMobile

This notification apparently pops up at the top of the Settings menu. It also includes a graphic showing how many hours of battery life you have left and how much usage time you’ll gain if you enable battery-saving mode.

I can see this proactive alert being very useful for people who either forget to charge their phones or those who are very busy. That battery life graphic should also help you make up your mind about whether you need to charge your device straight away.

Either way, this charging alert seems like a very sensible addition to One UI 9.5. We hope other Android OEMs copy Samsung and implement this in their own software skins.

items.title: TCL CSOT unveils APEX and IJP OLED breakthroughs for the AI era at DTC 2026
items.summary: TCL CSOT showed off the future of display tech at DTC 2026.
items.body:

General technology

TCL CSOT unveils APEX and IJP OLED breakthroughs for the AI era at DTC 2026

TCL CSOT showed off the future of display tech at DTC 2026.

Brought to you by TCL CSOT

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 2:56 AM ET

•

TCL CSOT

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

A screen has a big impact on how a device feels to use. It determines how crisp text looks on your laptop, how smoothly fast-moving games appear on your monitor, how long your phone lasts on a charge, and whether the person next to you on the train can read your screen. OLED screens, in particular, need a lot of precision to manufacture, which is why they’re most often found only in higher-end phones, laptops, monitors, and tablets.

TCL CSOT, which makes and develops displays for many device manufacturers, is working on a method to build OLED panels by printing the materials onto them, which could help OLED get into more products.

At DTC 2026, its annual Global Display Tech-Ecosystem Conference in Wuhan, China, on November 13, TCL CSOT showcased its latest display tech: inkjet-printed OLED, a 500Hz gaming monitor, a 115-inch 16K screen that shows 3D without glasses, and more. They also took Android Authority on a tour of the Wuhan factory and the t12 production line, where they’re working on the IJP OLED. Here’s what you need to know.

How inkjet-printed OLED works

TCL CSOT

IJP OLED stands for inkjet-printed OLED. While traditional OLED manufacturing uses processes to deposit organic materials onto the display, IJP OLED uses specialized printers to place those materials precisely where they’re needed. The idea is similar to using a home inkjet printer, but the “ink” is made of organic materials that form a working OLED panel.

Printing the materials this way helps reduce waste and potentially lower manufacturing costs, which is a significant advantage for bringing OLED to a wider range of products in the future.

It also offers a picture-quality benefit. IJP OLED uses TCL CSOT’s Real Stripe RGB pixel arrangement, with separate red, green, and blue subpixels arranged in stripes. This design delivers sharper text and noticeably reduces color fringing around the edges of text and graphics compared with a conventional OLED panel.

TCL CSOT

Interview with Weiran Cao, Ph.D, at DTC 2026

With IJP OLED, we can reach 163 PPI on a 27-inch 4K display. For gaming displays, it can reach 218 PPI, with a 0.03 millisecond response time. People read a lot of text on monitors and laptops, so this is a benefit users can see every day.Weiran Cao, Ph.D, General Manager of IJP-OLED Middle Platform of TCL CSOT

TCL CSOT has already begun mass-producing IJP OLED panels, and several partner devices using this tech were featured at DTC 2026. The Lenovo Legion R9000P has a 16-inch IJP OLED panel with a 2,560×1,600 resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate, and 100% DCI-P3 coverage. Meanwhile, Lenovo’s ThinkVision P27UL-40 is the company’s first IJP OLED monitor for commercial use, with a 27-inch 4K display and 99% DCI-P3 coverage. The MSI Prestige 14 AI+ and MSI PRO MAX OLED 271UPJW12 also use TCL CSOT’s printed panels.

TCL CSOT has also introduced two new 14-inch IJP OLED notebook panels. One is less than 0.66mm thick, weighs under 66g, and has a reflectance of less than 1%. The other eliminates the cover glass, using a hardened polarizer with an 8H rating instead, but it still feels like glass to the touch, whether you use a finger or a stylus.

A 500Hz gaming monitor and a 115-inch 3D TV display

TCL CSOT

TCL CSOT showed off a 27-inch QHD gaming monitor featuring an IJP OLED panel with an oxide backplane, and supporting refresh rates of up to 500Hz. TCL CSOT says it’s the first display to use in-panel compensation for high refresh rates. It helps maintain picture quality and runs in real time in the background, so there’s no need for the periodic power-off cycles used by conventional methods.

Real Stripe RGB keeps edges sharp, with a response time under 1ms. The 500Hz refresh rate is designed for competitive gaming, keeping moving targets in fast-paced shooters crisp and easy to track.

TCL CSOT

The 115-inch display has a native 16K resolution of 15,360×7,680, and TCL CSOT says it is the world’s highest image quality 16K 2D/3D-compatible light-field TV display. Its light-field optical architecture addresses the viewing-angle limitations of conventional glasses-free 3D, offering a 90-degree viewing angle or more, extended depth of field, and support for multiple viewers, so you don’t have to sit in one specific spot. The 3D light-field resolution reaches up to 8K, and the screen can switch between 2D and 3D, with TCL CSOT claiming there’s no loss in 2D picture quality.

The recommended viewing distance is 2–4m (6.5–13ft), making it well suited for private theatres, digital museums, interactive gaming, and premium showrooms. It’s an impressive display, though it’s unlikely to find its way into living rooms anytime soon.

More efficient and more private mobile displays

TCL CSOT

The 6.36-inch blue phosphorescent OLED may have been one of the most practical displays at DTC 2026. TCL CSOT says it’s the first smartphone OLED display to use a blue phosphorescent material system, which they say delivers roughly 40% higher luminous efficiency and around 20% lower electroluminescent power consumption at the same brightness.

The display is a major power draw, so the battery-life improvements are definitely exciting. Paired with the larger batteries introduced in newer handsets, more efficient screens could significantly increase the time you can use your device between charges. TCL CSOT is also working to refine materials and manufacturing processes to extend device lifetimes and bring blue phosphorescent displays to more devices.

TCL CSOT

The World’s First Full-Angle Lossless Privacy OLED Tablet Display(10.95″) helps keep your screen private from people nearby. Its dual-pixel architecture and pixel-level light-path control provide 360-degree active privacy while keeping the view clear from the front.

APEX and AI for Real

TCL CSOT

All of these technologies are part of APEX, TCL CSOT’s advanced display technology brand, created with picture quality, eye comfort, and sustainability in mind. APEX is built on four pillars: Amazing Display Experience, Protective of Eye Health, Eco-friendly to Build and Use, and Unlimited Imaginative Potential.

AI for Real was another major focus at DTC 2026. TCL’s strategy is to bring AI out of the lab and into everyday life. For TCL CSOT, a key part of that vision is Display for AI — advancing display technology so AI-powered devices can deliver a better experience. Whatever an AI assistant does on your phone or laptop, the screen is where you see the results and respond. That means better displays can make AI features feel more useful in your day-to-day life.

Know more about TCL CSOT at DTC 2026

TCL CSOT

At DTC 2026, TCL CSOT showed off its progress on several fronts. IJP OLED is moving beyond the demo stage and toward mass production, while gaming panels are advancing toward 500Hz. The company also showcased a 115-inch glasses-free 3D screen, along with new mobile panels that use less power and help keep your screen private. Bringing these efforts together is AI, which is helping TCL CSOT design displays much faster. And the great news is that many of these features are already in everyday use.

TCL CSOT makes panels for other device makers, so you can find its technology in products from a range of brands. IJP OLED is already featured in Lenovo and MSI laptops and monitors showcased at DTC 2026. The other displays are currently technology demonstrations, with no retail timelines announced yet. You can find more information about TCL CSOT’s display technology on its website.

At DTC 2026, its annual Global Display Tech-Ecosystem Conference in Wuhan, China, on November 13, TCL CSOT showcased its latest display tech: inkjet-printed OLED, a 500Hz gaming monitor, a 115-inch 16K screen that shows 3D without glasses, and more. They also took Android Authority on a tour of the Wuhan factory and the t12 production line, where they’re working on the IJP OLED. Here’s what you need to know.
How inkjet-printed OLED works
TCL CSOT

IJP OLED stands for inkjet-printed OLED. While traditional OLED manufacturing uses processes to deposit organic materials onto the display, IJP OLED uses specialized printers to place those materials precisely where they’re needed. The idea is similar to using a home inkjet printer, but the “ink” is made of organic materials that form a working OLED panel.
Printing the materials this way helps reduce waste and potentially lower manufacturing costs, which is a significant advantage for bringing OLED to a wider range of products in the future.

It also offers a picture-quality benefit. IJP OLED uses TCL CSOT’s Real Stripe RGB pixel arrangement, with separate red, green, and blue subpixels arranged in stripes. This design delivers sharper text and noticeably reduces color fringing around the edges of text and graphics compared with a conventional OLED panel.
TCL CSOT
Interview with Weiran Cao, Ph.D, at DTC 2026

With IJP OLED, we can reach 163 PPI on a 27-inch 4K display. For gaming displays, it can reach 218 PPI, with a 0.03 millisecond response time. People read a lot of text on monitors and laptops, so this is a benefit users can see every day.Weiran Cao, Ph.D, General Manager of IJP-OLED Middle Platform of TCL CSOT

TCL CSOT has already begun mass-producing IJP OLED panels, and several partner devices using this tech were featured at DTC 2026. The Lenovo Legion R9000P has a 16-inch IJP OLED panel with a 2,560×1,600 resolution, a 240Hz refresh rate, and 100% DCI-P3 coverage. Meanwhile, Lenovo’s ThinkVision P27UL-40 is the company’s first IJP OLED monitor for commercial use, with a 27-inch 4K display and 99% DCI-P3 coverage. The MSI Prestige 14 AI+ and MSI PRO MAX OLED 271UPJW12 also use TCL CSOT’s printed panels.

TCL CSOT has also introduced two new 14-inch IJP OLED notebook panels. One is less than 0.66mm thick, weighs under 66g, and has a reflectance of less than 1%. The other eliminates the cover glass, using a hardened polarizer with an 8H rating instead, but it still feels like glass to the touch, whether you use a finger or a stylus.
A 500Hz gaming monitor and a 115-inch 3D TV display
TCL CSOT

TCL CSOT showed off a 27-inch QHD gaming monitor featuring an IJP OLED panel with an oxide backplane, and supporting refresh rates of up to 500Hz. TCL CSOT says it’s the first display to use in-panel compensation for high refresh rates. It helps maintain picture quality and runs in real time in the background, so there’s no need for the periodic power-off cycles used by conventional methods.
Real Stripe RGB keeps edges sharp, with a response time under 1ms. The 500Hz refresh rate is designed for competitive gaming, keeping moving targets in fast-paced shooters crisp and easy to track.
TCL CSOT

The 115-inch display has a native 16K resolution of 15,360×7,680, and TCL CSOT says it is the world’s highest image quality 16K 2D/3D-compatible light-field TV display. Its light-field optical architecture addresses the viewing-angle limitations of conventional glasses-free 3D, offering a 90-degree viewing angle or more, extended depth of field, and support for multiple viewers, so you don’t have to sit in one specific spot. The 3D light-field resolution reaches up to 8K, and the screen can switch between 2D and 3D, with TCL CSOT claiming there’s no loss in 2D picture quality.

The recommended viewing distance is 2–4m (6.5–13ft), making it well suited for private theatres, digital museums, interactive gaming, and premium showrooms. It’s an impressive display, though it’s unlikely to find its way into living rooms anytime soon.
More efficient and more private mobile displays
TCL CSOT

The 6.36-inch blue phosphorescent OLED may have been one of the most practical displays at DTC 2026. TCL CSOT says it’s the first smartphone OLED display to use a blue phosphorescent material system, which they say delivers roughly 40% higher luminous efficiency and around 20% lower electroluminescent power consumption at the same brightness.

The display is a major power draw, so the battery-life improvements are definitely exciting. Paired with the larger batteries introduced in newer handsets, more efficient screens could significantly increase the time you can use your device between charges. TCL CSOT is also working to refine materials and manufacturing processes to extend device lifetimes and bring blue phosphorescent displays to more devices.
TCL CSOT

The World’s First Full-Angle Lossless Privacy OLED Tablet Display(10.95″) helps keep your screen private from people nearby. Its dual-pixel architecture and pixel-level light-path control provide 360-degree active privacy while keeping the view clear from the front.
APEX and AI for Real
TCL CSOT

All of these technologies are part of APEX, TCL CSOT’s advanced display technology brand, created with picture quality, eye comfort, and sustainability in mind. APEX is built on four pillars: Amazing Display Experience, Protective of Eye Health, Eco-friendly to Build and Use, and Unlimited Imaginative Potential.

AI for Real was another major focus at DTC 2026. TCL’s strategy is to bring AI out of the lab and into everyday life. For TCL CSOT, a key part of that vision is Display for AI — advancing display technology so AI-powered devices can deliver a better experience. Whatever an AI assistant does on your phone or laptop, the screen is where you see the results and respond. That means better displays can make AI features feel more useful in your day-to-day life.
Know more about TCL CSOT at DTC 2026
TCL CSOT

At DTC 2026, TCL CSOT showed off its progress on several fronts. IJP OLED is moving beyond the demo stage and toward mass production, while gaming panels are advancing toward 500Hz. The company also showcased a 115-inch glasses-free 3D screen, along with new mobile panels that use less power and help keep your screen private. Bringing these efforts together is AI, which is helping TCL CSOT design displays much faster. And the great news is that many of these features are already in everyday use.

TCL CSOT makes panels for other device makers, so you can find its technology in products from a range of brands. IJP OLED is already featured in Lenovo and MSI laptops and monitors showcased at DTC 2026. The other displays are currently technology demonstrations, with no retail timelines announced yet. You can find more information about TCL CSOT’s display technology on its website.
